text: Room opened — goal: accessibility: Make EXCAVA usable by EVERYONE — contrast, mobile/touch, reduced-motion, keyboard nav, scr

name: Ramp
text: Add a single high-contrast skip link at the top of every page that only appears when keyboard focus arrives. This solves the biggest keyboard navigation pain point—traversing repetitive headers—without cluttering the interface for mouse users. The trade-off is one extra DOM element per page, but it’s invisible to sighted mouse users and costs almost nothing in performance.

name: Reader
text: The real risk is sighted keyboard users will still overlook the skip link if it’s visually distinct only on focus—it’s invisible until they tab, so they may not realize it exists. A better alternative is a persistent skip link that’s always visible but visually subtle, paired with a brief on-screen cue (like a small icon) so all users know it’s there. Test this with both sighted and screen-reader users to settle it—if keyboard users still miss it, the alternative wins.

name: Ramp
text:
Add a persistent skip link at the top-left of every page, styled in high contrast but subtle until focused. This balances discoverability for sighted keyboard users with minimal visual clutter for mouse users. The trade-off is a small but constant visual element, but it removes the risk of users missing the skip link entirely.

name: Reader
text: Persistent skip links still get ignored—sighted keyboard users treat them as noise. A better alternative is a one-time onboarding hint (e.g., “Press Tab to skip headers”) that appears only on first visit, then fades. Settle it with A/B testing: track how often users actually use the skip link versus the hint.

name: Access
text: DECISION: Implement a one-time onboarding hint that appears only on first visit, then fades, to inform users about the skip link. The result must deliver a significant increase in skip link usage, and the lead developer owns the implementation and A/B testing to validate its effectiveness.
